title: Beyond Spectroscopic Strong Coupling: Operational Benchmarks for Cavity-to-Magnon Quantum Transfer
authors: Huang Xinyi, Zhang Xiang, Zhao Dongxing
abstract: Normal-mode splitting reveals coherent cavity--magnon hybridization but does not certify finite-time quantum-state transfer. We describe quantum transfer in a passive, linear cavity--magnon system coupled to thermal reservoirs as a thermal-loss channel specified by its coherent transmissivity $η$ and output-referred thermal population $ν$. For single-rail qubits, we calculate the phase-corrected average fidelity and compare it with the deterministic measure-and-prepare benchmark of $2/3$. A Bell pair shared by the cavity and an isolated reference retains reference--magnon entanglement if and only if $η>ν$. An input squeezed vacuum of strength $r$ yields sub-vacuum magnon fluctuations if and only if $ν<η(1-e^{-2r})/2$. When the initial magnon and both reservoirs have the same occupation, an analytically determined peak-transmissivity time optimizes all three tasks. These task-dependent benchmarks show that a conventional linewidth-based strong-coupling criterion does not guarantee quantum-transfer performance. Conversely, entanglement or squeezing can survive below that spectroscopic reference when the added noise is sufficiently low. These benchmarks provide quantitative targets for transfer timing and thermal-noise control in intracavity-to-magnon quantum interfaces.
summary: This paper develops rigorous, operational benchmarks to quantify quantum-state transfer efficiency between a cavity photon mode and a magnon mode. It demonstrates that standard strong-coupling criteria based on spectroscopy are insufficient predictors of actual transfer performance. The results provide quantitative guidelines for controlling thermal noise to ensure high-fidelity quantum information transfer in cavity magnonics.
main_problem: To establish operational benchmarks for quantum-state transfer from an intracavity photon mode to a magnon mode, moving beyond simple spectroscopic strong-coupling criteria.
main_result: Conventional linewidth-based strong-coupling criteria do not guarantee quantum-transfer performance; entanglement or squeezing can survive below these spectroscopic thresholds if noise is low enough.
method: The authors analyze the system dynamics using open-system master equations and derive time-dependent quantum channels, comparing fidelity and entanglement survival against theoretical benchmarks.
model_or_system: The system is a passive, linear cavity–magnon system coupled to independent Markovian thermal reservoirs, described by an interaction Hamiltonian and analyzed via Langevin equations.
key_observables: Phase-corrected average fidelity ($F_{avg}$), reference–magnon entanglement survival, and the presence of sub-vacuum magnon fluctuations.
important_parameters:
Coherent transmissivity ($\eta$), output-referred thermal population ($
u$), and the coupling strength ($g$) relative to cavity/magnon decay rates ($\kappa, \gamma$).
main_assumptions: The system is treated as a passive, linear coupling, and the thermal reservoirs are assumed to be independent and Markovian.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the three transfer tasks, steady-state cavity occupation vs. bath temperature, spectroscopic thresholds, and time evolution of cavity occupation.
paper_structure: The paper moves from defining the physical system and the limitations of spectroscopic criteria to deriving quantitative benchmarks based on fidelity, entanglement, and squeezing survival, culminating in task-dependent performance metrics.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial quantitative metrics for assessing the viability of quantum interfaces, showing that simple spectral measurements are insufficient for guaranteeing high-fidelity quantum information transfer in realistic, noisy environments.

Spintronics.note: The new paper analyzes quantum-state transfer between a cavity photon mode and a magnon mode, which directly falls under the scope of quantum-optics concepts applied to magnetic systems (magnons coupled to cavity photons).
